newsitem.title: GERMANY: G7 leaders say strong dollar should now hold steady.
newsitem.headline: G7 leaders say strong dollar should now hold steady.

text.p: The world's top financial leaders, gathering in Berlin for a summit meeting, sent out strong signals to currency markets on Saturday that while they favoured a strong dollar, the U.S. currency had now risen far enough.

Some of the finance ministers and central bank governors from the Group of Seven (G7) most-industrialised countries stressed that they were comfortable with the dollar's recent gains, which had been actively sought by the group itself.
But they made it equally clear that what was now needed was for exchange rates to remain stable at current levels.
"...the dollar correction process ought to end about now," said Hans Tietmeyer, the head of the powerful German central bank, the Bundesbank, before the summit talks began at 1110 GMT.
The finance ministers and central bank governors of Germany, Britain, Canada, France, Italy, Japan and the United States are taking part in the summit.

The meeting is taking place in the Kronprinzenpalais, the building formerly used by the east German government to entertain foreign government officials and at which the Treaty joining the two halves of Germany was signed in 1990.
The agenda covers a wide range of themes including the world economic outlook, Europe's single currency plans, debt relief for poor nations and increased bank surveillance.

But a surge of over seven percent in the dollar's value since the start of the year, seen by some G7 members as potentially harmful because of the speed of the change, put currency rates firmly on the top of the agenda.
Although there had appeared to be some difference of opinion on the dollar gains in advance of the meeting, officials arriving in Berlin spoke as with one voice.
French central bank head Jean Arthuis added his support to Bundesbank's view.
"I would like the new configuration of foreign exchange rates to be stable and lasting," he said.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, using the language adopted by the G7 itself to urge the dollar's recovery from all-time lows hit in spring 1995, said: "The orderly reversal sought by the G7 has taken place".

Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka made clear that he backed this position. Japan has been increasingly uneasy about the dollar's rapid progress as it threatened to increase its already high trade surplus and could prompt selling of Japanese assets by international investors.
Europe seemed less concerned, as the dollar's rise has boosted exports and lifted growth at a time when countries rush to cut budget deficits in time to launch a single currency in 1999.

Strong dollar has also helped the United States, keeping import prices low and helping to maintain low inflation, though U.S. carmakers are beginning to squeal about the negative effect of the dollar's rise on their exports.
And there are indications that the U.S government, long an advocate of ever stronger dollar, also views current levels as appropriate.
In a subtle change of tone for the United States, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin noted on Friday the currency had been strong "for some time now".
His comments sparked a dollar sell-off on Friday evening, highlighting market sensitivity to any hint the U.S. currency's rise may be overdone.
In yet another indication of the degree of understanding on the issue, Bundesbank's Tietmeyer said on Saturday Rubin's comment was "important."
The four European countries at the talks were also expected to brief their G7 partners on progress towards monetary union.
